questions.stem: Where one of two vessels is to keep out of the way, what must the other vessel do first?
options: Alter course to starboard
Keep her course and speed
Slow down to let the give-way vessel pass
Sound one prolonged blast
questions.explanation: Rule 17(a)(i): the stand-on vessel keeps her course and speed, so the give-way vessel can plan around a predictable target. Altering or slowing at this stage can spoil the give-way vessel's action.

questions.stem: When MAY the stand-on vessel take action to avoid collision by her manoeuvre alone?
options: At any time she judges it convenient
As soon as it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action
Only when collision is certain
Only after the give-way vessel answers her signal
questions.explanation: Rule 17(a)(ii) allows the stand-on vessel to act once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action. Acting whenever convenient would break stage 1. 'Only when collision is certain' describes the later stage where she must act, not when she may.

questions.stem: The stand-on vessel finds herself so close that collision cannot be avoided by the action of the give-way vessel alone. What does Rule 17 require?
options: She may keep her course and speed because she has the right of way
She shall take such action as will best aid to avoid collision
She shall sound the doubt signal and hold her course
She shall turn to port
questions.explanation: Rule 17(b) makes action mandatory at this stage: 'such action as will best aid to avoid collision'. Holding course here breaches the Rules. A signal alone is not action, and the rule does not fix a direction (and a port turn is usually the worst choice for a vessel on your port side).

questions.stem: Which pair of words describes the two later stages of Rule 17 correctly?
options: Stage 2 'shall', stage 3 'may'
Stage 2 'may', stage 3 'shall'
Both 'may'
Both 'shall'
questions.explanation: Stage 2 (give-way vessel apparently not acting) is permissive: the stand-on vessel may act. Stage 3 (collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone) is mandatory: she shall act.

questions.stem: You are a power-driven stand-on vessel in a crossing situation. The give-way power-driven vessel is on your port bow and is not altering. You decide to act under Rule 17(a)(ii). Which action should you avoid if the circumstances admit?
options: A large alteration to starboard
A substantial reduction in speed
An alteration of course to port
Sounding at least five short and rapid blasts
questions.explanation: Rule 17(c) says a power-driven vessel acting in a crossing situation shall, if circumstances admit, not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side. If the give-way vessel finally turns to starboard as she should, a port turn by you would bring you together. Turning to starboard, slowing and sounding the doubt signal are all sensible.

questions.stem: As stand-on vessel, you are in doubt whether a give-way vessel in sight of you is taking sufficient action. What sound signal does Rule 34(d) require?
options: One prolonged blast
Two short blasts
At least five short and rapid blasts, given immediately
One short, one long, one short
questions.explanation: Rule 34(d) requires a vessel in doubt whether sufficient action is being taken by the other to give at least five short and rapid blasts immediately. Two short blasts means 'I am altering my course to port', and one prolonged blast is the bend or underway-in-fog signal.

questions.stem: The stand-on vessel has taken action under Rule 17 because the give-way vessel was slow to act. Is the give-way vessel now relieved of her duty?
options: Yes, the duty passes to the stand-on vessel once she acts
No, Rule 17 does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way
Yes, if the stand-on vessel sounded a signal first
Only if the vessels are in a narrow channel
questions.explanation: Rule 17(d) states that the rule does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way. Both vessels may end up acting, but the give-way vessel's duty never transfers.
